[p. 1] Athletic ability discrepancy, risk- taking, and recovery quality as predictors of match-related injuries in adolescent soccer players Aynollah Naderi 1, Vahid Reza Kohe 2 & Luis Calmeiro 3 This prospective cohort study aimed to identify predictors of match-related injuries in 40 male adolescent soccer players (mean age 15.25 ± 0.87 years) across 20 regional league matches during the 2023–2024 season. Prior to each match, players completed validated assessments of mental fatigue, recovery quality, perceived match load, perceived injury risk, risk-taking behaviors, and athletic ability, with self- and coach ratings calculated to determine the Athletic Ability Discrepancy Score. Mental fatigue, match load, and perceived injury risk were not significant predictors (P > 0.05). Athletic ability was evaluated through both player self-ratings and coach ratings using a five-point Likert scale (1 = very low to 5 = very high) relative to same-age peers. The Athletic Ability Discrepancy Score was computed as Self-rating minus Coach rating of athletic ability. A positive score indicates the player rated themselves higher than the coach (potential overestimation), while a negative score indicates the player rated themselves lower (potential underestimation)27. To ensure data integrity and minimize peer influence, data collection was conducted individually in a private, controlled setting. Perceived risk level demonstrated a negligible difference (5.02%), and each unit increase in perceived risk was associated with a non-significant 7% increase in injury risk (OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 0.83–1.38, p = 0.61), suggesting that abstract risk perception—unanchored by prior injury experience—failed to translate into protective behavioral regulation in this cohort. Discussion This study aimed to investigate how training load, recovery quality, mental fatigue, perceived injury risk, risk-taking behaviors, and estimated athletic ability affect injury risk among adolescent soccer players. The main findings demonstrated that poorer recovery quality, greater engagement in risk-taking behaviors, and overestimation of athletic ability were each significantly associated with increased odds of sustaining a match- related injury in this cohort of adolescent soccer players. Among adolescent soccer players aged 14–17, 47.5% sustained new injuries, with an average of 0.65 injuries per player and an overall match injury incidence of 24.9 per 1,000 h of match exposure. This incidence is more than that reported in a systematic review by Robles-Palazón, et al.3, who found an average of 14.43 injuries per 1,000 match hours in male and female youth (≤ 19 years old) soccer players. In another review, Mandorino, et al40. also reported a wide range (2.84 to 47.7 per 1,000 h) in elite adolescent players, and Faude, et al 2. reported rates of 15–20 per 1,000 match hours in older adolescents. Such differences may reflect variation in competition level (elite vs. non-elite), age, and methodology. The lower injury incidence in our study may be due to the non- elite competition level, lower match intensity, and differences in exposure measurement methods. These factors should be considered when comparing injury rates across studies. Of the 26 injuries recorded, 61.5% were minimal (1–3 days of time loss), followed by mild (23.1%), moderate (11.5%), and severe (3.8%). These results align with Robles-Palazón, et al 3. and Faude, et al. 2, both of whom noted a predominance of minor injuries. Injury location data revealed that the most commonly affected sites were the thigh (30.77%), lower leg/Achilles tendon (19.23%), knee (15.38%), and ankle (15.38%), consistent with prior studies2,3,41. There was no significant difference in match load between injured and uninjured players, nor was there a clear association with injury risk. This contrasts with studies in adult populations 11,42,43, which found strong correlations between training loads and injury. The discrepancy may arise from age-related physiological differences, variations in measurement (e.g., subjective vs. objective load indicators), and our focus solely on match load rather than total load (training + matches) in our study than previous studies Gabbett and Domrow11and Anderson, et al. 42. These findings support the need for age-appropriate load management strategies that account for the developmental and contextual demands of adolescent athletes. Adolescent soccer players who remained injury-free reported significantly higher Total Quality Recovery (TQR) scores following both training sessions and games compared to those who sustained injuries. A one-point increase in the TQR score was associated with a 25% reduction in injury risk. Future studies should employ a priori power calculations, incorporate maturation metrics, expand surveillance to training contexts, and, where feasible, verify injury data through objective records. Conclusion This study found that overestimation of athletic ability, engagement in risk-taking behaviors, and poorer recovery quality were each significantly associated with increased odds of match-related injury in this cohort of adolescent soccer players. Unlike findings in adults, mental fatigue and perceived injury risk were not significant predictors in this young group, and match load alone did not predict match-related injury either. These results suggest the need for a comprehensive prevention approach that promotes realistic self-assessment, safe behaviors, and effective recovery strategies. Collaboration among coaches, trainers, and sports psychologists is essential to protect young athletes’ health and improve injury prevention. Future research should involve larger samples, longer follow-ups, and broader load monitoring to better understand match-related injury risk in youth soccer.
